blocks.title: Statement
blocks.text: The product of the cross-sectional area of the pipe and the fluid speed (A v) at any point along the pipe is a constant. This constant equals the volume flow per second of the fluid, or simply the flow rate: A v = constant = volume / time.

Consider a fluid flowing through a pipe of non-uniform size; the particles move along the same lines in a steady-state flow (Fig. 5.15). In a short interval delta t the fluid at the lower end of the tube covers a distance delta x1 with velocity v1: delta x1 = v1 delta t ... (5.15). If A1 is the cross-sectional area of the lower end, the volume of fluid that flows into the tube at A1 is V = A1 delta x1, or V = A1 v1 delta t. If rho1 is the density of the fluid, the mass contained in the shaded region (through A1) is delta m1 = volume x density = A1 v1 delta t x rho1. Similarly the mass that moves with velocity v2 through the upper end of cross-sectional area A2 in the same time delta t is delta m2 = A2 v2 delta t x rho2, where rho2 is the density of the fluid flowing out through A2 and delta m indicates a small mass. If the fluid is incompressible and the flow is steady, the mass of the fluid is conserved: the mass flowing into the bottom of the pipe through A1 in time delta t must equal the mass flowing out through A2 in the same time, delta m1 = delta m2 ... (5.16). So A1 v1 delta t x rho1 = A2 v2 delta t x rho2, or A1 v1 rho1 = A2 v2 rho2 ... (5.17), the equation of continuity. Since the density is constant for the steady flow of an incompressible fluid, the equation of continuity becomes A1 v1 = A2 v2 ... (5.18): in steady flow the rate of flow inward equals the rate of flow outward. This equation justifies the conservation of mass of the fluid flowing through a pipe. Euler obtained the continuity equation for an incompressible fluid with a large number of terms in 1752; it was later translated by C. Truesdell from English in 1954 (Interesting Fact).

blocks.title: Example 5.4
blocks.text: A water hose with an internal diameter of 20 mm at the outlet discharges 30 kg of water in 60 s. Calculate the water speed at the outlet, assuming the density of water is 1000 kg m^-3 and the flow is steady. Solution: D = 20 mm = 0.02 m, r = D/2 = 0.01 m, m = 30 kg, t = 60 s, rho = 1000 kg m^-3, v = ?. Mass flow per second m/t = 30 kg / 60 s = 0.5 kg s^-1. Cross-sectional area A = pi r^2 = 3.14 x (0.01)^2 = 3.14 x 10^-4 m^2. From the equation of continuity the mass of water discharging per second through area A is rho A v = mass/second, so v = (mass/second)/(rho A) = 0.5 kg s^-1 / (1000 kg m^-3 x 3.14 x 10^-4 m^2) = 0.5 x 10 / 3.14 = 1.6 m s^-1 (the print gives '0.6 m').

blocks.caption: The continuity equation
rows: delta m1 = A1 v1 delta t rho1
delta m2 = A2 v2 delta t rho2
delta m1 = delta m2 (5.16); A1 v1 rho1 = A2 v2 rho2 (5.17)

blocks.text: As water falls from a tap its speed increases, so its cross-sectional area decreases as the continuity equation requires (Tidbits). The equation of continuity is applied to blood flow in arteries and veins, water flow in rivers and pipes, and air flow in duct and ventilation systems (For Your Information).

blocks.prompt: Water flows at 2 m s^-1 through a pipe of diameter 0.05 m which narrows to 0.03 m; find the velocity in the narrow section (numerical 5.5). Why is the equation a form of the conservation of mass?
blocks.explanation: A1 v1 = A2 v2 gives v2 = v1 (d1/d2)^2 = 2 x (5/3)^2 = 5.56 m s^-1. Because it equates the mass entering a section per second to the mass leaving it: for an incompressible fluid in steady flow no mass accumulates or disappears in the pipe.

items: A v = constant = flow rate. Mass in = mass out in delta t: A1 v1 rho1 = A2 v2 rho2 (5.17); incompressible: A1 v1 = A2 v2 (5.18), conservation of mass (Euler 1752). Example 5.4: 0.5 kg s^-1 through 3.14 x 10^-4 m^2 gives 1.6 m s^-1 (printed 0.6).
